item.title: I run my local LLMs inside the ChatGPT desktop app now, and it took one free open-source tool to do it
item.itunes:title: I run my local LLMs inside the ChatGPT desktop app now, and it took one free open-source tool to do it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using the ChatGPT Desktop app recently, and as far as it was concerned, it's been talking to OpenAI's servers this entire time. In actuality, it's been talking to a combination of models through my OpenCode subscription, MiniMax M3, and even my local LLMs, like Qwen 3.8 27B and GLM-5.3-Flash.

Earlier this year, OpenAI rolled the Codex desktop application into the ChatGPT application, replacing it with a simple toggle that switches between using it for chat, or using it for coding. You can switch between individual projects, pick your models, or simply ask questions or have a conversation. You're restricted to OpenAI's models, naturally, but a free, open-source tool gives you access to way more than just OpenAI's models, and it's called opencodex.

opencodex is a pretty neat tool that works by proxying ChatGPT Desktop; you open the web UI, set up your models, and restart ChatGPT. On launch, it'll pick up all the regular OpenAI models alongside whatever you configured additionally, and it simply just... works.

opencodex pretends to be the OpenAI API, but it runs on your machine

Codex can simply use a different base URL

Codex ordinarily supports the OpenAI Responses API, but its base URL is configurable from your machine's environment variables. When you install and run opencodex, it modifies the ~/.codex/config.toml file to add the following environment variables, overriding the defaults:

# Auto-injected by opencodex
openai_base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:10100/v1"
# Auto-injected by opencodex
experimental_realtime_ws_base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:10100/v1"

What this does is fairly simple: when the Codex app looks to make a request, be it to list the available models, or send a chat message, it goes through the proxy first. To list the models, the proxy first contacts and aggregates the responses of any configured model providers, turning that into a list of available models that shows in the application. Then, when you select a model and send a chat message, it hits the proxy first which then decides where it gets routed to.

Models show up in the Codex model picker like normal, with my GLM-5.3-Flash showing up as "vllm/glm-5.3-flash", alongside all of the models from my OpenCode subscription that I've linked to it, too. The reason it exists as a proxy rather than a fork or modification of Codex is that translation survives Codex updates while also working with both the CLI and the desktop application, and despite installing a couple of Codex updates, it's continued to work just fine.

Installing opencodex is incredibly simple

A simple npm install command

To get started with opencodex, it's a simple npm install command to get both the proxy and the web dashboard up and running. You can use "ocx init" if you want a guided walkthrough to set up everything step by step, which writes the config, asks what provider you want, and offers to inject the config.toml file with the openai_base_url environment variable we mentioned above. Out of the box, it has support for models that are running on the same machine using the following runtimes on their default port:

  • Ollama
  • vLLM
  • LM Studio

However, you're not limited to just those options, as opencodex supports anything that supports either an OpenAI-compatible API or Anthropic's Messages API. It works over my private network, so I have different models that run on different machines all working through opencodex.

Once I had opencodex installed, adding my own model was really easy. I just created a new vLLM provider, added my DGX Spark cluster to it, and it automatically picked up GLM-5.3 Flash, which has been my go-to model as of late. In the web UI, I can also see token statistics, including individual API calls, estimated API costs, individual model usage, and more. It's really nice and easy to use, and it makes it possible to evaluate your token usage and see what you use the most.

Codex has weird tool calls, though

MiniMax M3 really struggled

Technically speaking, the claim that opencodex can use "any LLM" is correct, with the caveat that tool calls might decide whether your LLM can actually do anything with what you make available to it.

Codex has a rather unique tool calling structure. It has a freeform apply_patch for edits, shell access, MCP namespaces, and tool_search for discovery, and models which are trained on specific tool calling styles will flail when trying to use them. For example, when I tested MiniMax M3, it got totally, utterly lost.

GLM-5.3 Flash and Qwen 3.8 27B both handled it just fine, though, so it's not something that every model is going to struggle with. If a model you ordinarily use in the likes of Pi, Claude Code, or OpenCode works fine, but doesn't work in Codex, I'd first investigate whether it's correctly making tool calls or not. To be fair, every other model that I've tried has worked fine in Codex, and it was specifically MiniMax M3 that ran into issues like these. It definitely seems to be more of a niche problem, and for the majority of people, it should work just fine.

It's also important to be aware that web searches still go through OpenAI's servers, and so do vision requests if your model is setup as a text-only model. Models are given a "web_search(query)" tool to use, and when the model calls it, it uses GPT-5.6-Luna from your ChatGPT login to actually make the search. You can also configure Anthropic, xAI, Gemini, and Exa backends for search if you'd prefer.

Vision, meanwhile, works on a similar principle. If your model is a text-only model, a request containing an image goes to OpenAI's servers, identified, and then the text replaces what would have been the image in the prompt to the originally selected model. It's similar to what I did with my own shim layer for DeepSeek V4 Flash, but working through the Codex app instead.

If you try out a lot of LLMs or run local LLMs alongside your cloud models, opencodex is worth giving a try. It's a seamless experience in the Codex app, and it looks good, too. In my experience, models do fine with Codex-style tool calling syntax, but if they don't, you can always try switching to another model instead.

item.title: I stopped using my Fire TV Stick just for streaming after discovering these apps
item.itunes:title: I stopped using my Fire TV Stick just for streaming after discovering these apps
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I stopped treating my Fire TV Stick like a cheap streaming box the day I started sideloading APKs. And it turned out to be more capable than I expected. Its fate changed when I started removing ads and loading an Android launcher.

My experiments went further, and I stopped using the Fire TV Stick for streaming. Later, I found six apps that changed how I use my Fire TV Stick. None cost anything, and most are available in Amazon’s curated app store.

LocalSend made sure I didn’t need a USB cable

Moves files over Wi-Fi without touching a cloud account

While Downloader is a solid way to sideload apps on Fire TV Stick, finding the right code and typing it in is clunky. Instead, I use LocalSend on Fire TV Stick to send APKs, images, and other files from my phone, laptop, and home server. It’s like an AirDrop but with wider cross-platform support. The best part is that nothing routes through a third-party server.

I opened LocalSend on my phone and discovered the one running on my Fire TV Stick on the same network. Then, I sent files over HTTPS with an auto-generated certificate. It felt easier to push APKs than to use ADB from my laptop or home server. The only requirement is that I install it on every device where I want to send and receive files. Then it shows up under Nearby Devices within a few seconds. Surprisingly, this app is available on the Amazon Appstore.

TV Bro gives an actual browser experience

I installed it for the ad blocker

I've always missed a browser on Fire OS, and the Silk browser wasn’t cutting it. While Firefox is good enough for most users, I wanted a remote-friendly browser. That’s how I found TV Bro, an open-source browser built specifically for remotes. I can use tabs, bookmarks, voice search, and even a download manager without needing a mouse.

The built-in ad blocker strips out banner and video ads by default. The toolbar toggle lets me turn it off if a page breaks. It also blocks pop-ups and unwanted autoplay ads. I had to sideload this app through the Downloader, like other APKs, since it isn’t available in the Amazon Appstore.

Managing stick’s storage with AnExplorer

A proper file browser instead of the default settings menu

I transfer a lot of files to the Fire TV Stick and forget about it. I only try to remove those files when storage gets low, and that’s where AnExplorer helps most. This is my go-to file explorer on the Fire TV Stick, and it does a lot more than basic local browsing.

Beyond fetching files from local storage, AnExplorer offers several ways to source files. It offers SMB and FTP for home servers. It also supports cloud storage from Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Box. I can even unarchive ZIP and RAR files. That’s extremely useful while moving subtitles or ROM files. I set it as the default file picker so that I can easily open common archives and files.

TuneIn lets me use the stick even when the screen is off

Radio and podcasts run as audio in the background

I realized that even though the Fire TV Stick sits plugged into the TV, I don’t really need a display. That’s why I use TuneIn to stream live radio stations and also listen to popular podcasts. The audio keeps playing in the background even when the screen goes to sleep.

I leave the app streaming audio through the TV speakers while I work on something else in my room. The remote and Alexa are built for one thing at a time; TuneIn keeps playing while I do something else. The basic app is free, but it has ads that require a Premium subscription to remove. The subscription also adds a few exclusive stations and live sports radio.

Background Apps & Process List helps free memory

Force-stopping everything with a single tap

Unlike Android phones, the Fire TV Stick doesn’t have a "kill all apps" button or option. There’s no way to know what applications and services are running in the background. Like the app’s name, it lists every app and service that runs all the time. This app shows that list so I can force-stop one or all of them to free up memory.

Selecting an app from the list takes me to the App Info screen, where the Force Stop option is visible. Amazon Appstore has several similarly named apps that offer the same functionality. Stick with the listing that has the most reviews and an active developer. Force-stopping a system app can affect device stability. Doing that across every app on the list makes it worse.

Aerial Views to fetch video screensavers

Pull clips from self-hosted feeds or online libraries

This open-source app is available on the Amazon Appstore and even the Google Play Store. Once installed, I can choose the media sources to fetch screensavers from. For starters, I got access to hundreds of videos from Apple, Amazon, Jetson Creative, and Robin Fourcade. I found 4K videos with Dolby Vision since my LG C2 supports it. With a few ADB commands for the newer Fire OS, I installed Aerial Views in no time.

Besides replacing the default screensavers, it can pull up media from the USB drive, SMB or WebDAV shares. I can also import images from an Immich server and Nextcloud Memories. Using video screen savers helps with burn-in projection since the position of the on-screen overlays keeps shifting.

I replaced my Fire TV Stick with a mini PC, and now my TV does things Amazon never intended

Upgrading to a high-quality streaming experience.

9
By  Samir Makwana

Getting more out of the hardware than simply streaming

The Fire TV Stick is an Android device that Amazon has locked down by default. Every app on this list works around that limitation differently. It's about moving files, browsing the web without ads, managing local storage, monitoring memory, playing audio, or replacing the screensaver. If your Fire TV Stick is also sitting idle, you can use one of these apps to push it beyond generic video streaming.

item.itunes:title: I ditched Google Sheets for a self-hosted spreadsheet, and my data finally stopped leaving my network
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I use spreadsheets for all kinds of small tasks, from keeping track of projects to organizing information I need regularly. For years, Google Sheets was the obvious choice because it was quick, familiar, and worked from anywhere. But as I moved more of my software to my own setup, keeping important spreadsheets in someone else's cloud started to feel out of place.

I didn't want to give up the convenience of a browser-based spreadsheet. I just wanted a different way to run it. That's when I started experimenting with Grist. After moving a few of my everyday spreadsheets over, I realized it could fit surprisingly well into my workflow.

What is Grist?

It gives me the spreadsheet workflow I wanted

Grist is a relational spreadsheet-database app that I can host on my own server. When I first tried it, it felt familiar because the basic idea is still the same: I get rows, columns, cells, and tables that I can use to organize information. I came across Grist while looking for something that could replace the spreadsheets I use for everyday work. I mainly wanted a simple way to create tables, organize information, and keep track of things without dealing with a complicated interface.

The first thing I noticed was that Grist doesn't try to make spreadsheets feel completely different. I can start with a blank document, add columns, enter information, and use formulas just like I would in a regular spreadsheet. It also supports different ways of looking at the same information. I can work with a normal spreadsheet-style grid, but I can also switch to other views when that makes more sense for the information I'm working with.

I can build smarter spreadsheets

More ways to work with data

What I like about Grist is that it gives me more ways to work with a spreadsheet without complicating the basics. I can use features like filters, sorting, and conditional formatting to keep larger tables easier to manage. Forms have also become useful. Instead of opening the main table every time I want to add something, I can create a simple form and use it to enter new information. This makes some of my tracking tasks feel much more organized.

I can also add charts and summaries when I need a quick look at my information. This is useful when a table gets too long, and I want to understand what is actually in it. Another useful feature is the ability to customize how information is displayed on a page. I can arrange the elements I need and leave out the things that aren't important for a particular task.

NocoDB is the best self-hosted Airtable alternative for your home or business

Looking for a private, self-hosted app that can rival Airtable? NocoDB has got your back!

1
By  Ayush Pande

It does much more than Google Sheets

A spreadsheet with a database hiding underneath

The more I used Grist, the more I noticed that it wasn't really limited to the usual spreadsheet way of doing things. Underneath the familiar grid, it has features that make it work more like a simple database. I can connect information between tables instead of keeping everything in one large sheet. If I have a list of projects and another list of clients, I can link the two rather than entering the same client details repeatedly. This makes my information easier to keep organized as it grows.

Grist also lets me use reference columns to connect related records. I can then pull information from one table into another and use formulas to work with those relationships. This is probably the biggest difference I noticed compared with a traditional spreadsheet. I don't have to keep creating complicated formulas or duplicate information just because two sets of data are related. I still get the simplicity of a spreadsheet, but I can structure my information more carefully when a project needs it. For me, that's what makes Grist more than just another Google Sheets alternative.

Google Sheets replacement I actually control

My data stays inside my own network

This is where Grist became even more interesting to me. Since it is open source, I can run it myself instead of depending on a hosted spreadsheet service. I installed it on my own server with Docker, and now I have a spreadsheet tool running alongside the other services in my setup.

The biggest difference is where my data lives. My Grist documents are stored on my own server, so I don't have to send the information to Google's cloud every time I use a spreadsheet. I have control over the server, storage, backups, and who can access the application. I also don't lose the ability to work with other people. Grist lets me share individual documents and give others access when I need to collaborate.

That combination is what made the switch work for me. I get a familiar spreadsheet tool, but I can run it on infrastructure that I manage myself. For the kind of data I work with, that extra control is worth the small setup.

Forget about Excel - I self-host Grist to manage my spreadsheets

Step aside Excel, there's a new spreadsheet tool in town!

3
By  Ayush Pande

I didn't need another cloud spreadsheet

Switching to Grist wasn't about finding a perfect replacement for every Google Sheets feature. I wanted something that fit better into the way I already manage my software and data. After using it for my everyday spreadsheets, the switch feels surprisingly natural. Grist gives me enough flexibility for simple tasks while leaving room to grow when a spreadsheet becomes more complicated. For me, that's a trade-off worth making.

item.title: Cheap managed switches are the real networking upgrade nobody talks about
item.itunes:title: Cheap managed switches are the real networking upgrade nobody talks about
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When a home network starts feeling sluggish, the reflex is to buy a new router. Wi-Fi 7 routers are everywhere; the marketing is loud, and it feels like the obvious fix. But for most homes, the router is not the bottleneck, and a $500 flagship won't fix what's actually wrong.

The better upgrade costs about $30. A cheap managed switch gives you more wired ports, real network segmentation, and visibility into what your devices are doing, all things a router upgrade rarely touches. It's the unglamorous box that makes everything else on your network work better, and it'll outlive the next two routers you buy.

I put a 10GbE managed switch in my home, and here's what actually got faster

Bigger number, better... right?

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Your router probably isn't what's slowing your network down

The best Wi-Fi upgrade is actually less Wi-Fi

Most slow-network complaints come down to Wi-Fi, not routing. Walls, distance, neighboring networks, and a dozen devices all competing for airtime drag things down long before the router's processor breaks a sweat. A new router with a faster radio helps a little, but it can't change the physics of your house.

And the money goes to the wrong place. Current Wi-Fi 7 picks can be several hundred dollars, and a big slice of that pays for wireless throughput your phones and laptops can't use yet. That's a lot of cash for headline numbers.

Every device you move to a cable is one fewer device fighting for airtime. The TV, the game console, the desktop, and the NAS don't move, so they have no business being on Wi-Fi in the first place. Wire them up, and the devices that actually need wireless, like phones and laptops, get more of the spectrum.

The catch is that most routers ship with four or five LAN ports, and those fill up fast. A switch removes that ceiling. Even an unmanaged one does, but the managed kind brings a lot more to the party for barely any extra money.

Network switches will outlive your router

Wi-Fi standards change every few years, and the router gets swapped every time you chase the new one. A switch doesn't care. It'll sit in the closet as the backbone of your network for a decade, while routers, mesh systems, and access points come and go on top of it. It's the one purchase that keeps paying off through every upgrade after it.

YuanLey 6 Port 2.5G Network Switch

Managed switches aren't expensive anymore, and you can add plenty of ports and advanced features for not much money.

See at Amazon

What a $35 managed switch gets you

More advanced features than you'd think

Credit: 

The headline feature is 802.1Q VLAN support. The TP-Link TL-SG108E sells for about $25, supports 32 VLANs, and the Netgear GS308E is roughly the same price and supports 64. Both let you tag traffic and run a trunk to your router, which is the foundation for splitting your network into separate zones.

That matters most for smart home gear. Cheap cameras, smart plugs, and TVs with questionable update histories can live on their own VLAN, away from your laptop and your NAS. Guests get their own segment, and a home lab can have its own too. It's the kind of separation consumer routers rarely offer on their own.

You also get faster ports, with 2.5 GbE now the standard even on cheaper switches, and devices on the same switch can pass traffic between them without looping out to the router. PoE to power things like security cameras or access points is also another common feature.10 GbE still costs more, and you probably don't need it yet, but if you see a good deal, it's worth considering. Ethernet standards don't change as often as Wi-Fi ones, and 10 GbE will be relevant for years to come.

And then there's the managed aspect, with Quality of Service to better allocate your bandwidth, IGMP snooping to prevent multicast traffic from flooding every port on the switch, and link aggregation to bond two ports together for a more consistent experience when users access files on your NAS.

A $30 managed switch does what your $300 gaming router can't

I stopped trusting gaming routers for traffic management after learning what a managed switch actually does.

4
By  Jasmine Mannan

Cheap managed switches come with some strings attached

Budget firmware can be rough

The budget tier is usually sold as "easy smart" or "web managed," and that label is doing some heavy lifting. You get a web interface and the core features, but typically no command line, limited or no SNMP, and fewer VLANs and access controls than a proper managed switch. Some cheap "smart" switches only offer port isolation rather than true 802.1Q tagging, so check the spec sheet before you buy. For most homes, that's fine. For a serious homelab, you'll eventually outgrow it.

Security on these switches isn't great. A researcher's report on TP-Link's Easy Smart line found that the configuration utility broadcasts traffic using a static encryption key, and anyone on the same segment who captures and decrypts it can read the admin credentials in plaintext. With admin access, an attacker could rewrite the VLAN config and walk right out of the segment you built. The report lists at least 12 affected models, including the TL-SG108E, and says the underlying issue hasn't been properly fixed.

That doesn't make these switches useless, but it does change how you set them up. Change the default password, skip the desktop utility, and keep management access on a trusted VLAN that your IoT devices can't reach. Default VLAN 1 behavior can also be confusing on older hardware revisions, so plan your VLAN layout before you start clicking.

Most cheap 2.5 GbE managed switches use Realtek silicon, which is solid enough. The firmware can be wildly different. You could end up with a management interface with features that don't work, or even settings that don't stick after a reboot. They also draw more power, but only compared to unmanaged switches. Hardly a dealbreaker but worth knowing about.

I reverse engineered my cheap managed switch's firmware

People asked why I trust this Switch, so here's part of my process of reverse engineering it.

By  Adam Conway

Buy the switch first, then decide if you need a new router

A cheap managed switch won't make headlines, and it won't put a bigger number on your speed test. What it does is fix the problems that actually make home networks feel bad: too many devices on Wi-Fi, not enough ports, no separation between your laptop and a $15 smart plug, and no idea what anything is doing. For $25 to $90, that's a better return than almost any router on the market. Plus, wiring up any device that isn't meant to be mobile will take it off your Wi-Fi, which might give the rest of your devices enough airtime to breathe.

When a home network starts feeling sluggish, the reflex is to buy a new router. Wi-Fi 7 routers are everywhere; the marketing is loud, and it feels like the obvious fix. But for most homes, the router is not the bottleneck, and a $500 flagship won't fix what's actually wrong.

The better upgrade costs about $30. A cheap managed switch gives you more wired ports, real network segmentation, and visibility into what your devices are doing, all things a router upgrade rarely touches. It's the unglamorous box that makes everything else on your network work better, and it'll outlive the next two routers you buy.

I put a 10GbE managed switch in my home, and here's what actually got faster

Bigger number, better... right?

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Your router probably isn't what's slowing your network down

The best Wi-Fi upgrade is actually less Wi-Fi

Most slow-network complaints come down to Wi-Fi, not routing. Walls, distance, neighboring networks, and a dozen devices all competing for airtime drag things down long before the router's processor breaks a sweat. A new router with a faster radio helps a little, but it can't change the physics of your house.

And the money goes to the wrong place. Current Wi-Fi 7 picks can be several hundred dollars, and a big slice of that pays for wireless throughput your phones and laptops can't use yet. That's a lot of cash for headline numbers.

Every device you move to a cable is one fewer device fighting for airtime. The TV, the game console, the desktop, and the NAS don't move, so they have no business being on Wi-Fi in the first place. Wire them up, and the devices that actually need wireless, like phones and laptops, get more of the spectrum.

The catch is that most routers ship with four or five LAN ports, and those fill up fast. A switch removes that ceiling. Even an unmanaged one does, but the managed kind brings a lot more to the party for barely any extra money.

Network switches will outlive your router

Wi-Fi standards change every few years, and the router gets swapped every time you chase the new one. A switch doesn't care. It'll sit in the closet as the backbone of your network for a decade, while routers, mesh systems, and access points come and go on top of it. It's the one purchase that keeps paying off through every upgrade after it.

YuanLey 6 Port 2.5G Network Switch

Managed switches aren't expensive anymore, and you can add plenty of ports and advanced features for not much money.

See at Amazon

What a $35 managed switch gets you

More advanced features than you'd think

Credit: 

The headline feature is 802.1Q VLAN support. The TP-Link TL-SG108E sells for about $25, supports 32 VLANs, and the Netgear GS308E is roughly the same price and supports 64. Both let you tag traffic and run a trunk to your router, which is the foundation for splitting your network into separate zones.

That matters most for smart home gear. Cheap cameras, smart plugs, and TVs with questionable update histories can live on their own VLAN, away from your laptop and your NAS. Guests get their own segment, and a home lab can have its own too. It's the kind of separation consumer routers rarely offer on their own.

You also get faster ports, with 2.5 GbE now the standard even on cheaper switches, and devices on the same switch can pass traffic between them without looping out to the router. PoE to power things like security cameras or access points is also another common feature.10 GbE still costs more, and you probably don't need it yet, but if you see a good deal, it's worth considering. Ethernet standards don't change as often as Wi-Fi ones, and 10 GbE will be relevant for years to come.

And then there's the managed aspect, with Quality of Service to better allocate your bandwidth, IGMP snooping to prevent multicast traffic from flooding every port on the switch, and link aggregation to bond two ports together for a more consistent experience when users access files on your NAS.

A $30 managed switch does what your $300 gaming router can't

I stopped trusting gaming routers for traffic management after learning what a managed switch actually does.

4
By  Jasmine Mannan

Cheap managed switches come with some strings attached

Budget firmware can be rough

The budget tier is usually sold as "easy smart" or "web managed," and that label is doing some heavy lifting. You get a web interface and the core features, but typically no command line, limited or no SNMP, and fewer VLANs and access controls than a proper managed switch. Some cheap "smart" switches only offer port isolation rather than true 802.1Q tagging, so check the spec sheet before you buy. For most homes, that's fine. For a serious homelab, you'll eventually outgrow it.

Security on these switches isn't great. A researcher's report on TP-Link's Easy Smart line found that the configuration utility broadcasts traffic using a static encryption key, and anyone on the same segment who captures and decrypts it can read the admin credentials in plaintext. With admin access, an attacker could rewrite the VLAN config and walk right out of the segment you built. The report lists at least 12 affected models, including the TL-SG108E, and says the underlying issue hasn't been properly fixed.

That doesn't make these switches useless, but it does change how you set them up. Change the default password, skip the desktop utility, and keep management access on a trusted VLAN that your IoT devices can't reach. Default VLAN 1 behavior can also be confusing on older hardware revisions, so plan your VLAN layout before you start clicking.

Most cheap 2.5 GbE managed switches use Realtek silicon, which is solid enough. The firmware can be wildly different. You could end up with a management interface with features that don't work, or even settings that don't stick after a reboot. They also draw more power, but only compared to unmanaged switches. Hardly a dealbreaker but worth knowing about.

I reverse engineered my cheap managed switch's firmware

People asked why I trust this Switch, so here's part of my process of reverse engineering it.

Buy the switch first, then decide if you need a new router

A cheap managed switch won't make headlines, and it won't put a bigger number on your speed test. item.title: I found four obscure motherboard headers that serve almost no purpose, but manufacturers keep shipping them anyway
item.itunes:title: I found four obscure motherboard headers that serve almost no purpose, but manufacturers keep shipping them anyway
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Modern computing has come a long, long way. We went from AGP slots moving about 2GB/s and IDE ribbon cables wide enough to block half the airflow in case to a PCIe 5.0 x16 slot carrying roughly thirty times that bandwidth, storage wired straight into the CPU, and a single rear port that pushes 40Gbps of data and a display signal at once.

And yet, the same boards carry remnants of a much older era. I went through the manual for my MSI B650 motherboard and found headers that I had never paid attention to, let alone thought about using, because these were designed for accessories that haven't been in use for a while. Here are four motherboard headers that'll remind you of a bygone age and serve little to no purpose on a modern PC.

JCI1, or the chassis intrusion header

It detects if the computer case has been opened

On my motherboard, the chassis intrusion connector is labeled JCI1, but it still ships with a variety of SKUs labeled as "chassis intrusion" (on ASUS boards) and simply CI on Gigabyte boards bundled with the F_PANEL headers. It consists of two pins, and as the name suggests, the purpose is to warn the user that the chassis has been opened. It's possible to enable it even on modern boards via the BIOS's Chassis Intrusion Configuration.

The only issue is, I have neither owned nor seen a consumer case that shipped with a switch for it. The rationale is that it can serve a case for business and enterprise customers where IT professionals would want to be notified if the components inside a PC case have been tampered with. Tom's Hardware reported a case where this exact feature would've been useful back in August, where some thieves in Wuhan esports hotels swapped RTX 5080s for RTX 3060s, closed the cases back up, and went unnoticed for days. For most consumers with a personal computer, this one's going to sit unoccupied.

Credit: MicroStar International.
How to jump start or hotwire your PC using the motherboard headers

Knowing how to jump start your PC can save you loads of troubleshooting time and is also very easy

2
By  Ben Enos

JFP2 enables a troubleshooting tool from a bygone era

The oldest diagnostic tool on the PC, replaced by debug LEDs

If you've built or used a PC in the 2000s, you'll probably remember the beep when you hit the power button that confirmed a PC was booting. That sound came from a tiny plastic speaker wired to the motherboard, and JFP2 is the header it used to plug into. My manual lists it as a connector for the buzzer and speaker.

The speaker mattered because it woke up before the GPU did. If something was badly wrong with the PC, the monitor stayed black, and the beeps were the only way the board could report errors. Two beeps corresponded to one error, three meant another, and you could look the pattern up in the manual.

Cases stopped bundling that speaker many years ago, and boards found a clearer way to convey the same message. My B650M comes with EZ Debug LEDs sitting near the edge, and each covers a specific error that can stop a PC from booting. Red is the processor, yellow is the memory, white is the GPU, and green is the boot drive.

Credit: MicroStar International.
My motherboard's debug LED saved me hours of troubleshooting once I learned how to use it

Debug LEDs are good at debugging. Who knew?

By  Abhinav Raj

JTPM1 asks for a chip most CPUs already contain

Twelve pins for a security module that AM5 made redundant

JTPM1 is a 12-pin SPI header for a discrete TPM (Trusted Platform Module), of which three are simply marked as "Reserved." Every AM5 Ryzen already provides firmware TPM 2.0 inside the processor, so Windows 11 has no reason to look for a separate chip on the board. The header exists for buyers with policies requiring a physical module, and there's a market for it, though not one that overlaps with the people buying a micro-ATX gaming board.

That being said, it did have a brief moment of relevance. In March 2022, AMD confirmed that Ryzen systems could stutter intermittently with fTPM enabled, and advised users to fit a discrete TPM module instead while a BIOS fix was prepared. The fix came with AGESA version 1.2.0.7, and vendors shipped it from around May 2022.

Credit: MicroStar International.
These motherboard headers do something most PC builders never discover

Forget the usual headers — these connectors can be game-changing for your PC

1
By  Tanveer Singh

JDASH1 gets you a Tuning Controller that no one's selling

A header for a module no one buys

JDASH1 is labeled the Tuning Controller connector on the motherboard manual for my MSI B650M, which sounds useful until you look at what MSI puts on modern B650 boards. The manual says it connects to an optional Tuning Controller module, and sure enough, MSI does ship one with SKUs like the MEG Z890 Unify-X. It's a tiny module with a POST code display, power and reset buttons, OC retry and fail-safe buttons, and a clear CMOS button. It's essentially an external BIOS control panel of sorts for overclockers.

The problem, however, is that my B650M can't support the whole thing. JDASH1 on my SKU has six pins, and two of them do nothing. Pin 1 is blanked for keying and pin 2 is marked NC, which leaves an SMBus clock line, an SMBus data line, 5V and ground. On the motherboards that actually support this, the same header has fourteen pins that add the functionality to use OC retry and clear CMOS features. It is less than useless in this SKU.

Credit: MicroStar International.

The modern motherboard has some artefacts from the past

While most of these headers have no use for the average user who has built a PC around a modern chip for personal use, it costs manufacturers nothing to not remove them and some of them serve edge cases in other workloads, so I wouldn't be totally surprised if the next board I buy carries the same four. Standards are advancing everywhere else at the speed of light, but some headers inside the case remain, possibly for a trip down the nostalgia lane.

item.title: I made VS Code my writing and planning hub, not just my coding app
item.itunes:title: I made VS Code my writing and planning hub, not just my coding app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I never expected VS Code to replace some of the productivity apps I use every day, but that is exactly what happened. What started as a simple experiment to keep a few article drafts next to my coding projects quickly turned into a much bigger workflow change.

VS Code is still where I go when I need to work on code, but lately I spend just as much time using it as my writing desk, planning board, and personal productivity hub.

I rebuilt my VS Code setup from scratch this year, and it's the fastest it's ever been

My VS Code was drowning in extensions

By  Ayush Pande

I created one workspace for my entire writing workflow

Markdown turned VS Code into a proper writing app

The biggest change for me was creating a dedicated VS Code workspace instead of treating every article or client project as a random collection of files.

I now keep drafts, research notes, references, checklists, and supporting material under the same roof. It sounds simple, but it cuts down on app switching during the day.

Recently, I was working on a client website called Swami Jewels. Here, I need to keep track of website copy, product descriptions, SEO notes, technical requirements, and even database-related work for custom ring requests.

I can create a Swami Jewels workspace in VS Code with separate folders for copy, SEO, product pages, research, and development. I can have a homepage.md, about.md, and custom-rings.md sitting alongside a project checklist and technical notes.

Markdown is what really made this setup click for me. It keeps my environment clean. I can add headings, tables, links, bold text, quotes, and checkboxes without dealing with a busy formatting bar.

I can draft an entire product page in Markdown, structure it with H2s and H3s, add SEO notes at the top, include links to reference material, and maintain a checklist at the bottom.

Search and split view changed how I research and write

Flying through my workspace

Once a project starts getting bigger, VS Code’s search becomes useful. With Swami Jewels, I am not dealing with just one document. I may have homepage copy, product descriptions, SEO notes, custom jewelry pages, and development files sitting inside the same workspace. I can search the entire project in seconds.

Split view is another feature that changed how I write in VS Code. I often keep my main draft open on one side and supporting material on the other.

While working on Swami Jewels, I might have custom-rings.md open on the left and my SEO research or project brief on the right. That lets me check target keywords, project details, and tone guidelines without switching between docs at the top.

This setup is especially useful when I am rewriting something complex because I can compare the original copy with my new version side by side.

Extensions take the VS Code setup to the next level

A major strong point

The real power of VS Code starts showing once I bring extensions into the picture. I can easily add the functionality I need directly inside VS Code. For instance, when I am in the early stages of a project, I don’t always want to start with neatly organized paragraphs.

Sometimes, I need to throw ideas onto a canvas, connect different concepts, and figure out how everything fits together. Here is where I use the Excalidraw extension to brainstorm the website structure and visualize how different sections of the project relate to each other.

I can take visualization even further with Mermaid diagrams. Since Mermaid uses simple text syntax, I can quickly create flowcharts and diagrams without leaving my notes. For example, I can map the entire custom jewelry journey from a customer submitting a ring request to consultation, design approval, and final delivery.

Then there are extensions that bring Kanban-style project management directly into VS Code. I can create columns for ideas, research, writing, review, and move tasks between them as the project moves.

Of course, it can’t replace Trello, but for my small projects, it gets the job done.

4 VS Code forks built for specific tasks

The classic VS Code is great and all, but these specialized forks are better for certain programming tasks

By  Ayush Pande

AI fits naturally into the workflow

The new Agents Manager view is amazing

AI is another reason VS Code works so well as my productivity hub. Since my drafts, research, project notes, and supporting files already live inside the workspace, I can bring an AI agent directly into the context instead of copying information back and forth.

I can ask it to summarize research, refine an outline, brainstorm alternative headings, clean up rough notes, and even create a quick website mockup for the upcoming client meeting.

The newer Agents window takes this further. It gives me a centralized place to start, monitor, and review agent sessions across projects.

VS Code runs my daily workflow

VS Code is still a coding app at heart, but I no longer think of it as just a coding app. Once I started using Markdown, workspaces, folders, extensions, search, and a few simple planning tricks, it quietly became one of the most useful productivity tools on my desktop.

Of course, it will not replace every dedicated writing or project management app, and I don't need it to. For my workflow, the real appeal is having fewer apps, fewer distractions, and one flexible workspace that handles far more than I expected.

item.title: I switched from Arduino IDE to ESPHome for my custom ESP32 smart home devices, and my projects got a lot easier
item.itunes:title: I switched from Arduino IDE to ESPHome for my custom ESP32 smart home devices, and my projects got a lot easier
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever since the prices of Raspberry Pi single-board computers hit deranged levels, I’ve found myself gravitating towards the ESP32 lineup for my DIY smart home gadgets. But as much as I hate to admit it, I was somewhat intimidated by these microcontrollers when I first bought an ESP32 module years ago.

You see, I’d started my ESP32 journey with Arduino IDE, and while it’s definitely helped me get some C++ practice in, I had to put in a lot of effort just to pull sensor readings from it, let alone use it to build complex automations. Fortunately, I came across ESPHome Device Builder a few years ago, and it just clicked with me instantly. Now, I won’t go so far as to say that it can replace the Arduino IDE for every ESP32 project. But when it comes to designing DIY smart gizmos for my Home Assistant server, I’d use ESPHome over Arduino IDE any day.

ESPHome’s reliance on YAML makes it extremely easy to use

Its detailed docs are really useful when pairing random sensors with the ESP32

As much as I adore the powerhouse that’s C++, spending hours working on long blocks of code was not something I wanted to do just to grab the temperature readings from a cheap weather sensor hooked up to an ESP32. Of course, I really appreciate the ability to tinker with low-level code for complex circuitry projects, but being forced to write multiple lines of code, only to end up with conflicts because I used the wrong function with the wrong library, was enough to deter my teenage self from ESP32 projects.

ESPHome, on the other hand, streamlined the experience so much that I’d sometimes take longer to connect the sensors to my ESP32 than actually writing the code. That’s because ESPHome uses YAML as the primary language for writing config files, and generates the equivalent C++ firmware under the hood. While YAML definitely has its quirks, it’s significantly easier to tinker with than C++, to the point where I’ve had projects where a handful of lines would be enough to pull the necessary metrics from my sensors.

It also helps that ESPHome has extremely detailed documentation covering everything from the run-of-the-mill sensors I’d find on cheap kits to wacky modules designed for specialized tasks. The current ESPHome Device Builder web UI also has a lot of menu-based elements corresponding to my code, and it’s so useful that I can easily configure different components for my ESP32 projects without writing a single block of code. The same holds true for troubleshooting, as I can just edit the variables of a conflicting code block from the accompanying menu.

The best part? ESPHome also supports C++ code, so I can use YAML for general syntax and switch to C++ lambdas when I want the extra flexibility of loops and conditional logic. Combine that with the ability to create automations using simple menu-based elements without leaving the ESPHome page, and you can see why I immediately switched to this platform from Arduino IDE.

Connecting custom ESP32 devices with HASS is just as simple on ESPHome

It also helps me manage multiple ESP32 (and even Raspberry Pi Pico) microcontrollers

I control all my smart gadgets and IoT paraphernalia from Home Assistant, and this includes everything built with ESP32 systems. On Arduino IDE, I’d have to use extra libraries and scripts to connect my ESP32 creations with Home Assistant over MQTT. It’s not impossible to pull off, but it adds extra work on top of the extra C++ coding complexity.

ESPHome, on the other hand, makes pairing my ESP32-powered projects with Home Assistant a breeze. Once ESPHome is done flashing the microcontrollers, Home Assistant’s automatic network discovery functionality picks it up, and I can configure the rest from the Devices & Integrations tab of the Settings page. And since all the sensors hooked up to my ESP32 are detected as entities, I can create all sorts of wacky automation pipelines with them.

Another neat perk of ESPHome Device Builder is its ability to manage multiple ESP32 (and even Raspberry Pi Pico) modules simultaneously. Sure, I can create different Arduino IDE windows, connect each one to different ESP32 units, and save the project files. But working on multiple ESP32 projects is a lot easier on a centralized ESPHome interface, where I can glance at the connection status, check recent logs, and run OTA updates for every microcontroller in my arsenal.

That said, Arduino IDE has a lot of utility in embedded projects

Although I’m not very fond of using Arduino IDE for smart home projects, things are a lot different when it comes to circuitry, embedded, and robotics experiments. Writing all the C++ code manually may be a hassle, but it allows for minimal overhead in projects with strict memory constraints. The same holds true for experiments where I need precise timings down to the last millisecond for the sensors, resistors, motors, and other accessories hooked up to my ESP32.

ESPHome

item.title: 4 Android Auto problems that turned out to be my phone's fault, not the car's
item.itunes:title: 4 Android Auto problems that turned out to be my phone's fault, not the car's
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I love using Android Auto and have done so for many years now. It completely replaced vehicle infotainment systems that are often sluggish, underpowered, and sometimes downright useless.

If you've ever tried using the built-in car navigation system, you'll know precisely what I'm on about, unless you drive a Tesla or a recent Volvo. Wireless Android Auto is even better, negating the need for the cable, but I've found some problems with the software that turned out to be the phone's fault.

Poor internet connectivity

Even while at home and in range of Wi-Fi

The issue with Android Auto Wireless is that it handles your phone's wireless connections. It uses both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi to connect your smartphone to the available device or car infotainment system. This helps ensure everything works as seamlessly as possible, without interruption, lag, or poor performance. There's a caveat, aside from the absolute decimation of battery life: internet connectivity.

We have a wireless access point in the garage that provides internet access to the front yard and driveway. The issue is that the phone can't connect to it because it's linked to the Android Auto receiver, so the fallback option is the mobile data connection. That wouldn't normally be a problem, but we live in the middle of nowhere, and the nearest mast is some distance away. That means as soon as my phone connects to my truck, it's game over.

No setting up Waze. No starting a Jellyfin music playlist that isn't available offline. No quickly finding somewhere to visit before setting off. I have to do all of this either before I turn on the vehicle or after we set off and get a better signal.

Android Auto is better when you disable most of your smartphone features

Keep your eyes on the road.

7
By  Rich Edmonds

The entire setup is hacked together

It's actually quite ridiculous

My vehicle is the Maxus T90 EV with CarPlay support. There's no Android Auto. Why? Good question. Actually, there is Android Auto support, but it's seemingly locked behind a software update, which I have so far been unable to get flashed onto my vehicle. Maxus' network of dealerships near me is nonexistent, which makes getting the job done almost impossible. I encountered a solution, however, in the form of an Android Auto to CarPlay wireless adapter.

This ingenious little device takes the wireless Android Auto connection, translates it to Apple CarPlay, and then outputs it to the Maxus T90 EV center screen. It's Android Auto running as Android Auto via CarPlay. Still with me? This means that sometimes the connection doesn't engage; there's sometimes a pop-up on the screen asking for authentication with a QR code even though scanning it does nothing. Aside from that, it's been flawless.

That said, should I encounter anything, it's likely due to the phone or the setup I have going. This isn't the vehicle's fault. I'm trying to get it to do something it simply wasn't designed to do.

3 easy fixes that completely eliminated my Android Auto lag

Using a faster, higher-quality USB cable, updating your device, and freeing up RAM can help Android Auto run more smoothly.

2
By  Patrick O'Rourke

ColorOS is a little too aggressive

Battery management taken to a whole new level

The Oppo Find X6 is a brilliant phone, but it can be seriously aggressive when it comes to letting apps use the battery with background processes. I had to manually approve each one so I can have WhatsApp notifications through, Home Assistant can alert me to high humidity readings, and other useful pings. But even then, it's not reliable enough that everything comes through. Some WhatsApp conversation notifications don't make it. The same with Home Assistant.

That also affects Android Auto, which is an unusual workload itself. The phone will be locked and on charge, all while using Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, music playback, mobile data, and navigation, all at once. That's quite the solution for ColoOS's battery management. I had to remove all restrictions for all apps used through Android Auto. But it also meant that when things go wrong, restarting the phone, disconnecting the dongle, and clearing the Android Auto cache became the norm.

Troubleshooting became more of a headache

Too many moving parts within the moving vehicle

Before, especially with wired Android Auto, connectivity issues usually landed with the phone or the infotainment. Now, since the setup is essentially hacked together using Android as a mediator, troubleshooting is much harder. In essence, we have Android Auto on the phone, wireless connected to an Android device, which then connects to the vehicle, pretending to be an iPhone. It's amazing but also terrible when it comes to figuring out what's gone wrong.

I still love using Android Auto

Android Auto has become one of those things I simply have to do before setting off. It's akin to strapping myself in, turning the vehicle on, and checking mirrors before setting off. Using the phone with the vehicle has become part of the journey, enhancing almost every aspect of each drive, but sometimes things go wrong, and because it's not natively supported by my truck, it can become infuriating.

I gave up on wireless Android Auto because the convenience isn’t worth the headache

When it comes to long road trips, wired is the only way to go.

28

No setting up Waze. No starting a Jellyfin music playlist that isn't available offline. No quickly finding somewhere to visit before setting off. I have to do all of this either before I turn on the vehicle or after we set off and get a better signal.

Android Auto is better when you disable most of your smartphone features

Keep your eyes on the road.

7
By  Rich Edmonds

The entire setup is hacked together

It's actually quite ridiculous

My vehicle is the Maxus T90 EV with CarPlay support. There's no Android Auto. Why? Good question. Actually, there is Android Auto support, but it's seemingly locked behind a software update, which I have so far been unable to get flashed onto my vehicle. Maxus' network of dealerships near me is nonexistent, which makes getting the job done almost impossible. I encountered a solution, however, in the form of an Android Auto to CarPlay wireless adapter.

This ingenious little device takes the wireless Android Auto connection, translates it to Apple CarPlay, and then outputs it to the Maxus T90 EV center screen. It's Android Auto running as Android Auto via CarPlay. Still with me? This means that sometimes the connection doesn't engage; there's sometimes a pop-up on the screen asking for authentication with a QR code even though scanning it does nothing. Aside from that, it's been flawless.

That said, should I encounter anything, it's likely due to the phone or the setup I have going. This isn't the vehicle's fault. I'm trying to get it to do something it simply wasn't designed to do.

3 easy fixes that completely eliminated my Android Auto lag

Using a faster, higher-quality USB cable, updating your device, and freeing up RAM can help Android Auto run more smoothly.

2
By  Patrick O'Rourke

ColorOS is a little too aggressive

Battery management taken to a whole new level

The Oppo Find X6 is a brilliant phone, but it can be seriously aggressive when it comes to letting apps use the battery with background processes. I had to manually approve each one so I can have WhatsApp notifications through, Home Assistant can alert me to high humidity readings, and other useful pings. But even then, it's not reliable enough that everything comes through. Some WhatsApp conversation notifications don't make it. The same with Home Assistant.

That also affects Android Auto, which is an unusual workload itself. The phone will be locked and on charge, all while using Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, music playback, mobile data, and navigation, all at once. That's quite the solution for ColoOS's battery management. I had to remove all restrictions for all apps used through Android Auto. But it also meant that when things go wrong, restarting the phone, disconnecting the dongle, and clearing the Android Auto cache became the norm.

Troubleshooting became more of a headache

Too many moving parts within the moving vehicle

Before, especially with wired Android Auto, connectivity issues usually landed with the phone or the infotainment. Now, since the setup is essentially hacked together using Android as a mediator, troubleshooting is much harder. In essence, we have Android Auto on the phone, wireless connected to an Android device, which then connects to the vehicle, pretending to be an iPhone. It's amazing but also terrible when it comes to figuring out what's gone wrong.

I still love using Android Auto

Android Auto has become one of those things I simply have to do before setting off. It's akin to strapping myself in, turning the vehicle on, and checking mirrors before setting off. Using the phone with the vehicle has become part of the journey, enhancing almost every aspect of each drive, but sometimes things go wrong, and because it's not natively supported by my truck, it can become infuriating.

I gave up on wireless Android Auto because the convenience isn’t worth the headache

When it comes to long road trips, wired is the only way to go.

item.title: A tiny 11x11cm mini PC runs my entire media center and smart home for less than one prebuilt NAS
item.itunes:title: A tiny 11x11cm mini PC runs my entire media center and smart home for less than one prebuilt NAS
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When setting up my home server, I wanted a reliable, always-on core to manage my smart home and media library. When looking at prebuilt 4-bay NAS enclosures or dedicated automation servers, the price tags were around $800 before you even consider hard drives. So, instead of buying a locked-down appliance or building a bulky, power-hungry desktop tower, I looked at mini PCs instead and found the GEEKOM A5 2027.

For a fraction of the cost, this tiny 11 x 11 cm chassis hid quietly behind my TV and pulled barely 10 to 25W at idle. Realistically, you don't need an expensive enterprise-grade rack-mount server or a bloated prebuilt NAS to run a robust home lab. By repurposing a value-packed, energy-efficient mini PC, you can build a lightning-fast media center and smart home hub without having to fork out over $1,000.

9 Docker containers that run 24/7 on my $100 mini PC

Maximum value budget homelab.

18
By  Samir Makwana

The specs are important

Don't pick up the cheapest machine; it might not be powerful enough

When it comes to self-hosting and home automation, the hardware specs of the machine you pick are pretty much fundamental. The reason I opted for the GEEKOM A5 2027 edition is that it's powered by the AMD Ryzen 5 7430U. It has 6 cores, 12 threads, and runs up to 4.3GHz. That means it can easily handle multi-container Docker deployments, Plex 4K hardware transcoding, and Home Assistant automation engines without worrying about thermal throttling, which matters a lot on small devices.

Unlike high-TDP gaming mini PCs that can scream and whine under load, a smaller, more compact 15W to 25W mobile silicon architecture means that you get near-silent operation as well as smaller electrical bills (even when you're running the device 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year). You might overlook this when you're looking for hardware, but having a PC you can hear over the movie you're playing can be frustrating.

While budget mini PCs often solder components down, the GEEKOM A5 features dual upgradable DDR4 SO-DIMM slots supporting up to 64GB, as well as native M.2 NVMe storage expandability. This means you can grow your container volumes and scratch disks whenever you like.

What can you use your mini PC for?

It can replace multiple home lab devices

Realistically, with the right hardware, a single mini PC can replace three or four separate dedicated home lab devices. You can set it up as a media core to run Plex, Jellyfin, or an ARR stack. By using AMD Radeon Vega graphics for hardware-accelerated video decoding, you can run Plex or Jellyfin alongside automated media-acquisition containers and smoothly stream 4K content to multiple local devices.

You can also use it as the brain behind your smart home, as running Home Assistant natively or via Proxmox virtualization means you can tie in local Zigbee/Z-Wave USB coordinators to manage lights, climate, and security with zero cloud latency. It essentially becomes the powerhouse behind all of your home automation.

You also have access to an internal vault. You can host self-hosted password managers, local file sync, and ad blocking, plus reverse-proxy routing behind a single static local IP.

How to set up your mini PC

Getting started isn't as simple as switching it on

Unfortunately, setting up your mini PC as your home media center and smart home hub isn't as simple as switching it on and being ready to go. You'll need to make a few adjustments during setup. Begin by wiping the device clean and choosing your hypervisor. Strip out or bypass default Windows 11 Pro and install Proxmox VE as a bare-metal hypervisor, or you can flash Home Assistant OS directly if you're dedicating the device entirely to automation.

You might also want to provision your storage mounts. A challenge with mini PCs is they don't have internal room for 3.5-inch hard drives, but you can fix this by pairing the GEEKOM A5 with a multi-bay USB 3.2 Gen 2 enclosure or direct-attached storage. Attach your external media storage pool, configure ZFS or EXT4 formatting, and map persistent storage volumes. This isn't fundamental. It just depends on how much storage capacity your mini PC already has, and if you want to expand it, you can always do that later, so you don't have to fork out so much money to begin with.

Lastly, it's time to deploy the containerized services. You can spin up Portainer or Docker Compose stacks for your media server, download clients, and monitoring tools as well. And with that, you're ready to go.

Geekom A5 2027

If you're looking for a high quality Mini PC that doubles as a smart home hub and a media centre then the Geekom A5 2027 is a great option thanks to its amazing specifications and budget friendly price point.

Sometimes a mini PC is the better option

You don't need an expensive enterprise-grade budget to build a powerful, responsive home cloud. By leveraging the efficient compute of a modern office mini PC like the GEEKOM A5 2027, you get enterprise-level automation and media capabilities for a fraction of the cost. Stop overpaying for bloated, locked-down commercial smart hubs and NAS appliances. Instead, you can pick up a versatile mini PC and take full control of your digital home without buying multiple devices.

item.title: Steam Cloud hit its limit, so I built a better sync system with my home server and two free tools
item.itunes:title: Steam Cloud hit its limit, so I built a better sync system with my home server and two free tools
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One of the worst parts of playing your favorite single-player titles across multiple machines is carrying your save games across all of them. It's largely a solved problem with games on Steam with virtually all games supporting cloud saves, but even in the cases where it does, I've run into instances where I can't rely on it, and one in particular sent me over the edge.

I play an unhealthy amount of Football Manager, and the latest game, Football Manager 26, does support syncing via the Steam Cloud, but there's a limit to how much data it's willing to carry across to other devices. I hit that limit awhile ago, and it silently stopped syncing one of my latest saves, which I only found out about after I had already left for a bout of travel. When I got home, I decided now was as good of a time as ever to set up game save sync through my home server with Ludusavi and Rclone, and it was way easier than I thought.

5 amazing self-hosted apps for gamers

Fancy yourself a home labber and a gamer? Here are five gaming-oriented services you can run on your local hardware

2
By  Ayush Pande

Games can outgrow their limit, and some don't even support Steam Cloud

A method to sync those games is a must

Football Manager syncs a bit differently to other Steam games. Once you hit save in the cloud location, the save only uploads once the player exits the game. There seems to be a 10GB limit on cloud saves, which is a number you can hit faster than you think, especially if you have a particularly long save or you just like to have a few going at once. This is a common problem you'll see reported all over the FM26 community, and it finally caught up to me.

One of my saves was too big for the cloud buffer, and I didn't really give it any notice until I was away from home, tried to load it, and found myself many months behind where I had left off before in-game. I could, of course, just bring a USB stick with me everywhere, or even upload to Google Drive or Dropbox as many players do, but I decided to put my home server to use as a sync location for all my game saves, not just FM.

Linux gaming is getting faster because Windows APIs are becoming Linux kernel features

As time goes on, fewer games than ever are unplayable on Linux

18
By  Ty Sherback

Ludusavi does the copying for me

An excellent backup tool

Ludusavi is a free, open-source tool that knows where thousands of games keep their saves, using data sourced from PCGamingWiki. It found Football Manager 26 on my laptop and desktop without any custom configuration, along with a handful of other games.

On its own, Ludusavi backs up to a local folder. What turns it into a cloud sync tool is its Rclone integration, which can push backups to any Rclone remote. I pointed mine at an SMB share on the Samba container on my Proxmox server, backed by a dedicated dataset on my ZFS pool. With automatic synchronization on, Ludusavi checks whether the local and server copies match before each backup, then uploads the new backup afterward. If the copies don't match, it warns me instead of overwriting anything.

I run a 32GB GPU instead of paying for Claude or Codex, and Qwen 3.6 keeps up more than I expected

Local LLMs are good enough for many tasks

22
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Reaching my server from anywhere

NetBird takes care of that

At home, syncing between devices is automatic with this setup already, but getting it to cooperate while I'm away from home is the bigger challenge. Thankfully, I have external access like this almost entirely sorted out. Since my SMB share doesn't expose itself to the internet at all, the method I use to access it is via a mesh VPN, and for this, I use a self-hosted deployment of NetBird.

NetBird allows me to access the entirety of my home server via WireGuard, and through the control plane, I've set the Samba share up as a network resource rather than an actual peer, which saves me another install and overall simplifies the deployment. My Proxmox host simply forwards the traffic it receives from my laptop or any other device wanting to access my saves to the LAN address of the LXC. And because my laptop uses the same LAN address to access at home and away in this instance, the single Rclone configuration covers both.

My entire family replaced Google Drive with Syncthing, and here's how I set it up

Bye-bye, Google Drive. Hello, private family cloud.

22
By  Yash Patel

Windows to Linux syncing takes one extra step

It still works, but there are some hoops

My laptop (usually) runs Windows, and my desktop runs CachyOS, where Football Manager 26 runs through Proton because it has no native Linux version. So the same save lives at two very different paths: my Documents folder on Windows, and a Windows-style Documents folder buried inside the game's Proton prefix on Linux.

Ludusavi won't restore a Windows path on Linux (or the reverse) until you tell it how the two map to each other. That's what redirects are for. On the desktop, I added a redirect that maps the Proton prefix's Documents folder to my Windows Documents path, so backups from both machines show the save the same way.

My outdated Windows 10 PC was headed for the recycling bin until Proxmox gave it a second life

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

An easy way to supply cloud sync when there isn't another option

Steam Cloud has mostly solved the issue of carrying your saves with you from place to place, but there are limits to it. In some cases, these limits are literal size limits, and in others, it simply doesn't reach to non-Steam titles. Thankfully, my home server fills this gap without giving up any of the convenience that Steam already provides.

Ludusavi does the copying for me

An excellent backup tool

Ludusavi is a free, open-source tool that knows where thousands of games keep their saves, using data sourced from PCGamingWiki. It found Football Manager 26 on my laptop and desktop without any custom configuration, along with a handful of other games.

On its own, Ludusavi backs up to a local folder. What turns it into a cloud sync tool is its Rclone integration, which can push backups to any Rclone remote. I pointed mine at an SMB share on the Samba container on my Proxmox server, backed by a dedicated dataset on my ZFS pool. With automatic synchronization on, Ludusavi checks whether the local and server copies match before each backup, then uploads the new backup afterward. If the copies don't match, it warns me instead of overwriting anything.

Reaching my server from anywhere

NetBird takes care of that

At home, syncing between devices is automatic with this setup already, but getting it to cooperate while I'm away from home is the bigger challenge. Thankfully, I have external access like this almost entirely sorted out. Since my SMB share doesn't expose itself to the internet at all, the method I use to access it is via a mesh VPN, and for this, I use a self-hosted deployment of NetBird.

NetBird allows me to access the entirety of my home server via WireGuard, and through the control plane, I've set the Samba share up as a network resource rather than an actual peer, which saves me another install and overall simplifies the deployment. My Proxmox host simply forwards the traffic it receives from my laptop or any other device wanting to access my saves to the LAN address of the LXC. And because my laptop uses the same LAN address to access at home and away in this instance, the single Rclone configuration covers both.

Windows to Linux syncing takes one extra step

It still works, but there are some hoops

My laptop (usually) runs Windows, and my desktop runs CachyOS, where Football Manager 26 runs through Proton because it has no native Linux version. So the same save lives at two very different paths: my Documents folder on Windows, and a Windows-style Documents folder buried inside the game's Proton prefix on Linux.

Ludusavi won't restore a Windows path on Linux (or the reverse) until you tell it how the two map to each other. That's what redirects are for. On the desktop, I added a redirect that maps the Proton prefix's Documents folder to my Windows Documents path, so backups from both machines show the save the same way.
